title: First Paper: Stretchable Mesh Electrodes in ACS Nano
excerpt: Mesh electrode arrays with graphene microneedles — >60% channel activation, 200% strain survival, and low-cost microfluidic fabrication.
body: I'm grateful to share that my first paper work is now published in ACS Nano, focusing on stretchable mesh electrode arrays with graphene microneedles for 3D organoid interfacing.
Strain tolerance200%No delamination or LM leakage; 2,000 cycles
We attribute the performance to two factors:
• Mesh geometry — open-network TPU substrate distributes strain away from electrode sites while maintaining media perfusion for organoid health.
• Elastic microneedle contacts — graphene/TPU composite needles conform to irregular organoid surfaces without tissue penetration (confocal imaging confirmed ~100 μm gap, no puncture damage).

Lesson Learned
Early prototypes used SU-8 structures. They were stiff. The mesh approach only emerged after two failed iterations.

The microfluidic patterning strategy avoids cleanroom-intensive steps: 3D-printed PDMS templates, vacuum-assisted graphene paste injection, liquid metal (EGaIn) interconnect filling, and TPU solvent-casting — no CVD graphene transfer, photolithography, or metal deposition required.

This milestone reflects two years of iteration in Jiang's Lab at SUSTech — from rigid prototypes to the MESH-GRIP concept that anchors the manuscript. Getting the balance right between mechanical compliance and electrical performance took more rounds than I expected, but the outcome is solid.
Research is mostly failure dressed up as iteration. The paper is just the part where things finally work.
